Class CachedDao

java.lang.Object
iu.dao.CachedDao
All Implemented Interfaces:
IuDao
final class CachedDao extends Object implements IuDao
Adds a process-wide read cache to a IuDao.

Two caches that never overlap

The delegate keeps its own read cache, scoped to the transaction it was read in. This one is scoped to the process. They are consulted in different situations and never both answer the same read:

inside a transaction
The read is delegated, so it is answered by the transaction's own cache or by the database — never by this one. A transaction sees its own writes and a consistent view of everything else, and a value published by some other caller could honor neither.
outside a transaction
The read is answered by this cache, which resolves a miss on a pooled thread. That thread is in no transaction, so the delegate reads through to the database and its own cache stays out of the way.

A transactional read is still worth something to this cache: it has already paid for a value a later non-transactional reader would have to fetch again. It is therefore injected once the transaction commits, which costs no additional query.

Why everything waits for the commit

Invalidations and injections are both buffered and applied from Synchronization.afterCompletion(int), only on Status.STATUS_COMMITTED. Publishing either one earlier would be wrong in a different way.

An invalidation raised before its write commits discards entries that a concurrent reader immediately repopulates from the state being replaced, leaving the value the write was meant to supersede in place until it expires. An injection published before commit exposes uncommitted state, and exposes a value that never existed at all if the transaction rolls back.

Deferring both also settles the case of a transaction that reads a row it has itself written: at commit, the value it read is the committed one.

Sequence marks

A value read inside a transaction is published long after it was read, so it carries the mark taken before the read rather than being stamped at publication. An invalidation raised in between therefore still discards it, instead of being ordered behind a value it predates.

A write republishing the row it just wrote wants the opposite order, so it takes its mark after raising its own invalidation.

What a read publishes

A search publishes each row it read as a load of that row's own primary key, so a search populates the individual lookups for free. This needs no declaration: the @Id mapping already states which columns identify a row, and IuSqlBuilder.getPrimaryKeyProperties(Class) reads it.

Publication is skipped for any row whose mapped key is not fully resolved, so a projection that omits an id column, or an entity that declares no key, publishes nothing rather than publishing a row under a key no load would have produced.

Nothing cached is ever handed out

An uncached DAO materializes a fresh row for every read, so an application may modify what it reads. A cache would otherwise break that: it answers every reader with the one instance it holds, and a reader that modified it would be modifying what the next reader is about to receive.

So rows are copied at both boundaries. A read copies on the way out. A read or write that publishes a row the caller also holds copies on the way in, at the moment of the call rather than at commit, since the caller may go on modifying it in between.

An entity mapped as an interface pays none of this. Its rows materialize as immutable proxies over the values they were read with, so both the rows and the unmodifiable list holding them are shared as they stand, and one instance serves every reader. Mapping an entity as an interface is the cheapest way to cache it, and the difference grows with the size of the result.

Queries and statements the caller drives

The get* family hands back an unexecuted operation rather than a result, so there is nothing to cache at the moment of the call. Each is wrapped instead, and acts when the caller runs it.

getBeanQuery(Class, Map) and its siblings
Read the cursor once into a list, publish every row as a load of its own key, and answer from the list thereafter. These are generated from the entity mapping and select its full column list, so each row is the same complete entity a load would have produced.
getQuery(Class, String, Iterable) and getFactoryQuery(java.util.function.Function, String, Iterable)
Read once into a list and answer from it, but publish nothing. The SQL is the caller's, so a row may be a partial projection, or carry no entity at all.
getBeanUpdate(Object), getBeanInsert(Object) and getBeanDelete(Object)
Invalidate the entity type and the row's own key when executed, on the same terms as saveBean(Object) but without republishing.
getStatement(String, Iterable)
Passed through untouched. Raw SQL names neither an entity type nor a row, so there is nothing to invalidate by; IuDao's standing instruction to call clear() after modifying rows by other means still applies, and here it applies to a process-wide cache rather than a transaction-scoped one.

Reading a cursor to exhaustion is what allows a query to publish the rows it carried, and it is also the one place this layer changes a caller's memory profile: SqlQuery.getResults(int) still pages, but over rows that have already been materialized. A result set too large to hold in memory therefore needs a DAO built without a refresh TTL, where every operation is passed through unwrapped.

    • updateBean

      public void updateBean(Object bean)
      Description copied from interface: IuDao
      Updates the row matching an entity's key and evicts that entity type from the transaction-scoped cache.

      An entity whose mapped columns all match the database is left alone rather than reported as an error.

      An EffectiveDated entity is not modified in place: a new row superseding its current one is inserted instead, carrying the changed values and copying the rest. Nothing matching the entity's key means there is no row to supersede, which is reported as an error the same way it is for an ordinary entity.

      Specified by:
      updateBean in interface IuDao
      Parameters:
      bean - entity carrying both the new values and the key to match

    • getQuery

      public <B> SqlQuery<B> getQuery(Class<B> beanClass, String sql, Iterable<?> args)
      Description copied from interface: IuDao
      Gets an unexecuted query over caller-supplied SQL and its bind arguments, materializing each row by matching result-set column labels to the target type's properties.

      A mapped entity's labels are resolved through its @Column and @SqlColumn mappings; any label that resolves to no mapped property, and every label of an unmapped type, falls back to matching the property name ignoring case and underscores. Labels matching no property are ignored.

      A value is read as the type its column stores and converted to the type its member declares, reversing what IuSqlBuilder.getForSql(Object, String) does when binding the same member: a character column mapped to a boolean reads back "Y" as true, a timestamp column mapped to an Instant reads back as an Instant, and the single space standing in for null on a SpaceForNull column reads back as null. A member belonging to no mapped column is read as its own type.

      A class is instantiated through its no-argument constructor and populated through its setters, skipping values that would assign null to a primitive property. An interface is instead materialized as an immutable view of the row's resolved values: its getters return those values, getters for columns the query did not select return null or the appropriate primitive default, its default methods run as written, and any other abstract method throws UnsupportedOperationException. Such a view stays valid after the query is closed.

      Specified by:
      getQuery in interface IuDao
      Type Parameters:
      B - result type
      Parameters:
      beanClass - type to materialize, which need not be a mapped entity
      sql - SQL text to execute
      args - bind arguments in placeholder order; may be null or empty
      Returns:
      unexecuted query
